TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES LINDA H. BRITE AND
LINDA J. BURGESS AND THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

         The Comanche Nation (Nation) timely files these exceptions to the August 20, 2026

Proposal for Decision (PFD). 1 The Nation generally agrees that the PFD reaches the correct

decision to deny the Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (CCN) application based upon the

identified Notice defects. If the Public Utility Commission (PUC or Commission) adopts the PFD,

the Nation’s concerns about the Project’s impacts on cultural and historic sites will be wholly

alleviated. That said, should the Commission decide not to adopt the PFD’s recommended denial,

the Nation implores the Commissioners to recognize what was admitted and proven during the

hearing in this proceeding—that the Nation’s interests, and the public policy and public interest of

the State of Texas, 2 can only be protected through the use of tribal monitors during pre-construction

survey work and construction itself, as well as the imposition of the Best Management Practices

(BMPs) submitted in the Nation’s Reply Brief. Accordingly, the Nation excepts only to the PFD’s

findings and conclusions related to the BMPs portion of the PFD and urges the Commission to

order tribal monitors and the other BMPs set forth in the Nation’s proposed ordering paragraphs,

should the Commission grant the CCN amendment and adopt a route in its final decision.

                                 SUMMARY OF EXCEPTIONS

         The Nation asserts exceptions with respect to the PFD’s dismissal of the Nation’s evidence,

as well as evidence provided by other parties to the proceeding, regarding the substantial amount

of cultural resources in the Project area, many (if not most) of which have not yet been identified;

overlooks or dismisses the substantial evidence put forward in this case that clearly shows that

ordering paragraphs imposing BMPs pertaining to cultural resources are necessary, should the

Commission deviate from the ALJs’ recommendation and approve a route for the Project.

                          STANDARD FOR COMMISSION ACTION

         Texas law authorizes the Commission to change a finding of fact or conclusion of law if a

finding is not supported by a preponderance of the evidence. Tex. Gov’t Code § 2003.049(g). In

this case, despite ample pre-filed and hearing testimony, the PFD erroneously concludes that the

BMPs reflected in the PUC’s ordering paragraphs for electric CCNs are adequate for this Project.

This conclusion, or the decision to leave out ordering paragraphs that require tribal monitor

presence, is contrary to the preponderance of the evidence.

    I.   OTHER PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES (ISSUES 14–15)

         Contrary to the testimony and exhibits, the PFD concludes that the Commission’s

standard ordering paragraphs are adequate with respect to cultural and historic resources. 3 The

PFD finds the PUC’s recommended ordering paragraphs supply sufficient “mitigation measures”

addressing cultural resources and that the record lacks evidence on cost, benefit, reliability,

design, and schedule. 4 Even the PFD’s use of the phrase “mitigation measures” itself

demonstrates that the Nation’s position and arguments have not been properly weighed. The

 Nation is seeking largely preemptive, proactive best management practices to prevent harm (and

reduce burdens on Joint Applicants)—not to mitigate damage after it occurs. This illustrates a

fundamental misunderstanding on the part of the ALJs that warrants revisiting the Nation’s

arguments and evidence.

       The conclusion that the PUC’s standard ordering language provides adequate BMPs is

contrary to the evidence. And rather than citing record evidence, the PFD adopts Joint

Applicants’ briefing explanations that Commission precedent has not typically ordered additional

mitigation measures, finding them “unnecessary, impractical, or already addressed in the

standard language.” 5 Yet, as the opening pages of this PFD point out, no 765-kV transmission

line has been constructed in Texas—the Bell Project will be one of the first. 6

    A. The Evidence Shows the Need for Tribal Monitor Presence as a BMP During Pre-
       construction Survey and Construction

       The record evidence reveals the shortcomings of standard or previously employed

methodology. For example, Joint Applicants’ consultant has employed the same standard

methodology to identify cultural resources that has been used in prior PUC proceedings. 7 But

inadequate or faulty past precedent does not justify perpetuating such inadequate or faulty

practices—particularly where, as here, the best interests and public policy of the State of Texas

are at stake. Joint Applicants specifically cite to the “consistent” dataset 8 as adequate for

comparison. However, consistent does not equate to comprehensive or sufficient. As Joint

Applicants’ witness Russell Marusak admitted, absence from an archeological database does not

reviewing Texas Historical Commission records is insufficient in light of the extensive historical

presence of the Comanche in the Project area. As shown in Section II below, this extensive

presence is well documented in the hearing record. Furthermore, as he testified during the

hearing, PUC Staff’s witness John Poole is not aware of any proposed route that parallels

cultural features—even though, as Mr. Poole agreed, cultural resources and human remains are

less likely to be disturbed when a transmission line is built parallel to cultural features. 10

        Moreover, the testimony shows the need for additional BMPs based upon the

environmental assessment limitations. For example, Joint Applicants’ witness Russell Marusak

acknowledged the high potential for encountering cultural resources not yet identified within the

Project area. 11 “There have been no boots on the ground surveys for any portion of the study

area,” 12 and Joint Applicants “cannot and have not” ruled out the possibility that culturally

significant Comanche resources exist in the Project area. 13 Similarly, Mr. Poole agreed that

additional groundwork on any route may yield additional cultural resources. 14 Given those

circumstances, and the fact that Joint Applicants’ extremely limited pre-application cultural

resource identification process failed to yield significant historical or cultural resources data (and

was deficient, as described below), the record clearly reflects that there is a strong need to

include additional BMPs in the post-approval but pre-construction survey work and during the

construction process itself, should the Project be approved.

required; Mr. Poole agreed during the hearing that Comanche Nation Tribal members would best

know cultural resources encountered along any proposed route. 15 Mr. Marusak acknowledged

that the Comanche Nation has historical and cultural ties to the Project area and agreed that

Tribal consultation can help identify cultural resources that might otherwise be overlooked. 16 Mr.

Marusak also agreed that tribes (like the Nation) may possess knowledge regarding cultural

resources that have not been included in public databases or publicly recorded inventories. 17

Comanches are uniquely qualified to identify and evaluate Comanche cultural resources and their

significance. The egregiously narrow scope of Joint Applicants’ environmental assessment

compels a more thorough methodology for the pre-construction cultural resources survey to

protect the interests of the Nation, the public, and the State of Texas. Moreover, tribal monitor

presence is not only a BMP in this context; it will ultimately save Joint Applicants both time and

money. Involving tribal monitors will result in a more thorough and accurate cultural resource

survey, reducing the likelihood and frequency of inadvertent discoveries during construction and

enabling Joint Applicants to make necessary adjustments early in the process rather than facing

halted construction and delays when a previously unidentified cultural resource is encountered.

The survey design must include Comanche Nation-approved tribal monitors to better ensure that

Comanche cultural resources can be identified and protected. 18 Furthermore, Comanche Nation-

     B. Tribal Monitor Costs Are Insignificant to the Project Budget

        The record reflects costs associated with tribal monitor presence during a pre-

construction survey and line construction. For example, as Algonquin Consultants expert

witness Jack Rossen states, a tribal monitor typically costs $40–$70 an hour, plus travel and per

diem expenses. 19 Further, the record reflects that Joint Applicants were aware of these costs and

their witness agreed that such costs could be absorbed within the existing Project budget,

including contingencies. 20 Notably, Joint Applicants evaluated costs at the conclusion of the

hearing. In Table 1 on page 43 of their Initial Brief, Joint Applicants compare the costs (and

other factors) of the nine routes they identified as “routes of interest” based on the hearing. These

costs range from $1.665B to $1.755B, or a variation of $90M, 21 demonstrating that Joint

Applicants do not view $90M as a significant price difference. This analysis alone demonstrates

that the tribal monitoring cost would be immaterial and absorbable. As Mr. Poole described it,

the range of costs in this case “would be the cost of the entire transmission line in other cases.

We’re talking like a hundred million dollars. That’s a pretty significant cost, but not as a

percentage of the overall project.” 22 Furthermore, Joint Applicants “applied a contingency of 10

percent and 15 percent in the cost model.” 23 The purpose of this cost contingency is to cover “‘an

     C. Tribal Monitoring Benefits the Project

        The record not only addresses the costs associated with the proposed BMPs (including

tribal monitors) but also includes significant testimony about the benefits and the design of such

practices. 26

        The PFD’s recommendation for standard ordering language is simply insufficient to

protect the directly affected (and directly threatened) interests of the Comanche Nation, the

public, and the State of Texas. Furthermore, while the PFD suggests that the PUC-recommended

ordering paragraphs are sufficient, Mr. Poole agreed that the PUC has no legal prohibition on

ordering the use of tribal monitors. 27 Notably, neither Joint Applicants nor the Commission’s

staff presented evidence to controvert the Nation’s position or specifically challenged the need

for any of the CCN conditions the Nation seeks. And the PFD itself does not cite to hearing

evidence. Rather, it cites only to Joint Applicants’ concerns that the Commission finds “pre-

approval surveys,” 28 “unnecessary or already addressed.” 29 Moreover, several intervenors

expressed strong support for tribal monitors and the Nation’s other requested CCN conditions in

their briefing. 30

          Finally, the request for tribal monitors is not unprecedented within the 765kV line

projects. Specifically, in the Howard-Solstice Transmission Line Project, SOAH Docket No.

473-26-14355, the PFD included similar tribal monitoring provisions as the Comanche Nation is

seeking in this matter. These provisions include:

         1. Engage a tribal-approved monitor during initial field surveys and all ground-
            disturbing activities;

         2. Submit an Unanticipated Discovery Plan prior to construction to address how
            the Project will proceed in the event tribal resources are discovered during
            construction. The Unanticipated Discovery Plan should include notification
            protocols for the Comanche and Apache tribes, and require coordination with
            the tribal monitor in assessing cultural discoveries;

         3. When a Marker Tree is identified during cultural resource surveys, halt all
            construction until the Texas Historical Commission and tribal monitor have
            coordinated to complete field verification and document the tree through
            photographs and data collection methods meeting Historic American
            Landscape Survey standards; and

         4. Prior to removing redberry cedar, Pinchot's juniper, or Texas mountain laurel,
            allow the Comanche Nation to harvest these species used in their religious and
            cultural practices where feasible.

Again, this demonstrates that although the line project itself is unprecedented, the mitigation

measures the Nation seeks are not exceptional—even in the context of the 765kV lines.

                                     FINDINGS OF FACT

   1. The concept of “community values” includes values significant to affected communities.

   2. The Comanche Nation (“Nation”) is an affected community for purposes of this
      proceeding.

   3. In their efforts to provide notice to the public, Joint Applicants provided direct notice of
      the Project to 28 municipal governments and 15 county governments.

   4. As they acknowledge, Joint Applicants provided no notice to Tribal government officials
      of the Nation, an affected community.

   5. Joint Applicants did not notify, consult, or contact the Nation regarding the Project prior
      to the Nation’s intervention in this proceeding. Although Joint Applicants may have
      complied with the Texas Utilities Code and Administrative Code provisions specifically
      related to notice, by failing to notify an “affected community,” they failed to solicit key
      information from the Nation that would have better informed the Application and they
      failed to comply with the spirit of the law with respect to notice.

   6. The proposed Project stretches across a significant portion of Comanchería, the ancestral
      homelands of the Comanche that include a vast swath of present-day Texas.

   7. The Project area is rich with cultural and historical resources, many of which hold great
      cultural, historic, and spiritual significance to the Comanche Nation.

                                     FINDINGS OF FACT

    1. The concept of"community values" includes values significant to affected communities.

   2. The Comanche Nation ("Nation") is an affected community for purposes of this
      proceeding.

   3. In their efforts to provide notice to the public, Joint Applicants provided direct notice of
      the Project to 28 municipal governments and 15 county governments.

   4. As they acknowledge, Joint Applicants provided no notice to Tribal government officials
      of the Nation, an affected community.

   5. Joint Applicants did not notify, consult, or contact the Nation regarding the Proj ect prior
      to the Nation's intervention in this proceeding. Although Joint Applicants may have
      complied with the Texas Utilities Code and Administrative Code provisions specifically
       related to notice, by failing to notify an "affected community," they failed to solicit key
       information from the Nation that would have better informed the Application and they
       failed to comply with the spirit of the law with respect to notice.

   6 . The proposed Project stretches across a significant portion of Comancheria, the ancestral
       homelands of the Comanche that include a vast swath of present-day Texas.

   7. The Project area is rich with cultural and historical resources, many of which hold great
      cultural, historic, and spiritual significance to the Comanche Nation.

    8. Texas Historical Commission ("THC") records are not comprehensive and do not include
      all existing cultural and historical resources in the Project area.

   9. Despite conducting a review of THC records, Joint Applicants failed to properly identify
       at least three existing cultural resource trinomials within 500 feet of the proposed
       centerline of the transmission line, demonstrating that even the THC record review-the
       only cultural resources study done to date-was insufficient.

    10. Although the Nation did not have an opportunity to bring its concerns about the Project to
        the attention of Joint Applicants prior to this proceeding or influence the Environmental
        Assessment, interested individuals who responded to the public interest questionnaire
        identified numerous landowner and local government concerns related to archeological
       and historic sites and the presence of cultural resources along several portions of the
       proposed routes, putting Joint Applicants on notice that cultural resource protection is a
       community value that mandates consideration in this proceeding.

    11. Construction of the Project poses a significant risk of destruction or desecration of
        Comanche cultural resources.

    12. Any damage to Comanche cultural resources during construction of the Proj ect would
        harm the interests of both the Comanche Nation and the State of Texas.

    13. Any damage to Comanche cultural resources during construction of the Proj ect would
        violate the public policy of Texas.

    14. Tribal monitors are trained Native American representatives who observe construction,
       infrastructure, or environmental proj ects to protect cultural resources, ancestral sites, and
       human remains. They ensure compliance with cultural resource protection laws and
       inadvertent discovery plans, bridging traditional knowledge with modern archeology to
       identify tribally significant cultural resources and to prevent damage during construction.
       They are also used during projects to ensure that Indigenous knowledge and expertise are
       incorporated in cultural resources surveys, increasing the value and accuracy of a survey.

    15. The incorporation of Comanche Nation-approved tribal monitors during the pre-
        construction cultural resources survey will enhance the survey and willlikely result in
        more comprehensive, accurate, and thorough survey results.

    16. By improving the survey results, the incorporation of tribal monitors during the pre-
       construction cultural resources survey will minimize the number of inadvertent
       discoveries during Project construction and reduce costs and delays that result from such
       inadvertent discoveries.

    17. The services of tribal monitors during construction of the Project will protect cultural
       resources encountered during construction that have not been identified during the pre-
       construction survey.

                                PROPOSED CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

    1. State law requires that the State of Texas "locate, protect, and preserve all sites,
       objects,... and locations of historical [andl archeological... interest, including but not
       limited to prehistoric and historical American Indian or aboriginal campsites, dwellings,
       and habitation sites [andl archeological sites of every character..." Tex. Nat. Res. Code §
       191.002.

   2. The imposition of reasonable conditions on the amended CCN granted herein to locate,
      protect, and preserve Comanche cultural resources contained within the Proj ect area
      supports Texas public policy and promotes the public interest of the State of Texas.

   3. PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to consider community values and historical
      values in determining whether to grant a CCN. The Proj ect must be routed to the extent
      reasonable to moderate the impact on the Comanche Nation as an "affected community"
      pursuant to 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).

   4. The use of tribal monitors during a post-approval and pre-construction cultural resources
      survey and during construction of the Project will best ensure Joint Applicants'
       compliance with State law regarding the location, protection, and preservation of cultural
       and historical resources contained within the Project area.

   5. Joint Applicants demonstrated an ability to pay for the costs associated with tribal
      monitors during the cultural resources survey and during construction.

                          PROPOSED ORDERING PARAGRAPHS

       Consistent with the above Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, the Commission

issues the following orders.

    1. Joint Applicants must conduct a pre-construction cultural resources survey of the
       approved route prior to engaging in ground-disturbing activities.

   2. Joint Applicants must retain the services of Comanche Nation-approved tribal monitors to
      assist and participate in the pre-construction cultural resources survey at Joint Applicants'
       expense.
   3. Joint Applicants must retain the services of Comanche Nation-approved tribal monitors to
      conduct tribal monitoring during all ground-disturbing activities during construction of
      the Proj ect at Joint Applicants' expense.

   4. Joint Applicants must develop an Inadvertent Discovery Plan for construction of the
      Project in conjunction with the Comanche Tribal Historic Preservation Officer (THPO)
      and the THC that shall include, at a minimum, the following provisions:
